title: Francis Dana to Robert R. Livingston, St Petersburg, 6 Apr 1783 (O.S.), No. 23: eight lines in Dana's own Lovell-type table (key WIN)

documents.shelfmark: NARA RG 360, Papers of the Continental Congress, item 89 vol. 2 (M247), naId 502963402, MS p. 730 (digital object 315); triplicate, docketed 'Tript. No. 23'

plaintext.source: Wharton, Revolutionary Diplomatic Correspondence VI (1889) pp. 381-383 prints the clear text with '(Here follow eight lines of cipher.)' and no decipherment.

transcription.notes: Read twice from the scan, the second time independently; both readings agree token for token. 212 tokens measured with docs/_check_profile.py --measure --digits: 204 fully visible letter numbers, 4 code groups and 4 numbers cut by the microfilm frame edge (written n|, counted as distinct tokens). The ink blot in line 3 is not transcribed.

system.summary: Periodic numerical table of the Lovell type over a..z and & (27 signs), key word WIN with period 3, number = (p - K) mod 27 + 1; word numbers above 27 from Dana's own list of October 1782 (three numbers per word, 30-263, 264-305 blank), after which the key starts again. Four groups above 27 in No. 23: 31, 137 and 168 are read from the list, 29 is not in it.
system.sibling_key: Livingston's own cipher to Dana, which Dana says he laid aside (P.S. of No. 23; letter of 23 Sept 1782, Wharton V pp. 752-754); not used here.
system.notes: distinct_symbols = 27 table numbers and 4 code groups seen. nomenclator.entries counts the groups seen in No. 23, not Dana's list (78 words by the review's count, not transcribed here). 24 Nov 2026: 31 = Administration, 137 and 168 = Minister, from Dana's own table (PCC 89 vol. II p. 656); the table's example runs N, W, I and restarts at N after a word number, which is the reset described next. The rest of this note is of 27 Oct 2026. After each of 31, 137 and 168 the next letter is under N: the groups reset the key to N (the earlier 'No. 1' sheet prescribes such a restart after an arbitrary character). The text after the opening 29 starts under W, which the reset does not explain, so the opening [29]n an [31] is not confirmed.

prior_solution.where: 24 Nov 2026: the Hawkins transcripts (PCC item 109, naId 2316037) were checked for Dana's table (objects 103-104) and No. 23 (object 207): the transcript gives the cipher numbers, no decipherment. Earlier: Wharton VI (1889) prints the passage as cipher without decipherment; the key sheet 'No. 1' in PCC 59 vol. 1 pp. 137-138 is an earlier, different scheme (checked after the break); the Madison Papers note says it is not decoded there. Wharton VI p. 464 'The key to Mr. Dana's cipher is missing' belongs to Dana to J. Adams, 1 June 1783, not to No. 23. Original and duplicate of No. 23, the Hawkins transcripts, Giunta, the MHS Dana Papers and the Papers of John Adams vol. 13 (Dana to JA, 4 Oct 1782, and notes, which describe Dana's cipher) not checked. A parallel independent reading by Brice Dudout was published the same day as this one (Europe chiffrée, 27 Oct 2026): a blind break of the same three alphabets, then Dana's own table of October 1782 found at PCC 89 vol. II p. 656; neither used the other.

tools: index of coincidence over periods and alphabet sizes (solver's working script, not included)

solution.what: Located Dana's No. 23 in NARA PCC item 89 vol. 2 (naId 502963402): MS pp. 727-730, digital objects 312-315; the cipher on p. 730, docketed as the triplicate.
Transcribed the eight lines from the scan (212 tokens); four numbers cut by the frame edge marked n|.

Numbers 1-27 apart from four groups; index of coincidence over periods and alphabet sizes pointed to a 27-sign alphabet and period 3, but the signal is weak (period-3 IC 1.30 x 27 against 1.12-1.23 for other periods); the bigram ranking of the keys (control below) is what finds the key.
Shifts for the three positions found by scoring; in Lovell's convention (key letter = 1) the key word is WIN. Long English runs at each phase.

Aligned the text line by line: three encipherer slips (W positions enciphered with N, N, I), one skipped key position, four cut numbers completed from their first digit, three letters supplied at line ends from the key phase. 201 of 211 letter positions decode directly.

Independent re-reading of the scan and independent decryption script: same 212 tokens, same plaintext; found that the code groups move the key phase irregularly (after 31 and 168, not after 137; 29 opens the text), so the opening [29]n an [31] is not confirmed.

Bigram scores (repository English word list): decryption -2.739; 200 wrong keys with the same alignment best -4.431; all 19,683 period-3 keys on the raw uncorrected stream rank WIN second (WIP first, one letter off) and NWI tenth; 200 shuffles best -4.874.

Wharton V-VI read for the letter and Dana's cipher: No. 23 printed with '(Here follow eight lines of cipher.)'; the 'key ... is missing' footnote belongs to the letter of 1 June 1783 to J. Adams; the scan's P.S. reads 'has come to hand', Wharton 'has not come'. Two web searches found no decipherment.
Code groups 29, 31, 137, 168 considered from context (court, ministry, system); no value adopted, one occurrence each.

Review lead checked after the break: Dana's key sheet in PCC item 59 vol. 1 pp. 137-138 (naId 475671573, images 107-108, Fold3 172700-172701). It is headed 'No. 1': a 25-sign table (a..z without j and v, plus &) in three columns that are not the W, I, N alphabets, and a word list numbered 26-52 (England 29, Holland 31, ... Russia 51, Court 52). It is not the 27-sign WIN scheme of No. 23; 137 and 168 are not on it, and England / Holland do not fit '[29]n an [31] like this'. Verso: 'N.B. When you come to an arbitrary character begin [the] key word again.'

Phase after the code groups re-measured on the raw numbers: after each of 31, 137 and 168 the next letter is under N (liketh..., adopti..., herehe...); W and I give nonsense. So the groups reset the key to N, a fixed restart of the kind the No. 1 sheet's N.B. prescribes. After the opening 29 the text starts under W, which this rule does not explain.

Statistical validation (docs/_validate.py): 204 tokens, 58 types, en-modern order 4: reading -1.921 per letter; random keys -6.754 (z 11.8); key annealed onto shuffled ciphertext best -2.808 (mean -3.025, z 7.4); annealer on the real text -2.786. Verdict: pass.

Brice Dudout's parallel reading (https://bdudout.github.io/europe-chiffree/en/documents.html#dana-1783): he broke the three shifted alphabets blind (frequencies, English 4-grams), then found Dana's table of October 1782 at PCC 89 vol. II p. 656 (alphabets from n, w, i; nomenclator 30-305, three numbers per word; keyword restarts after numbers above 27), whose columns match the break. Values for the open groups: 31 Administration, 137 and 168 Minister, 29 a slip for i. Lines 1-5 agree with the reading here wherever both give a value. The sheet itself not yet viewed here.

Reading review of both entries for No. 23: reading.md and dudout/reading.md read as sentences against their decryptions; four coherent sentences each, completions and code groups marked; grade A recorded on each. Dana's 1782 table sheet was not viewed, so 31, 137 and 168 stay open in the first reading.

Andrew Beling (issue #898, with AI agents) located a transcript copy of Dana's table and of No. 23 in PCC item 109 (naId 2316037): objects 103-104, 'Mr Dana's Cypher' (NARA: 14 Oct 1782), with 'Administration 1 2 3' in block 30-122 (31, 62, 93), 'Minister 7 8 9' in block 123-215 (137, 168, 199), the example 'When the army of America go' and the rule 'begin your Key word anew. # Or to a Cypher above 27'; object 207, a clerk's transcript of No. 23 that gives every number in full: the 208 fully read numbers identical to ours, the four cut numbers 11, 15, 27, 26, the three line ends 20, 11, 1. 29 is in neither the alphabets nor the list. His statement that 216-305 have no words is wrong (next step).

Integration review (AI agent, for the maintainers) opened the NARA images by curl. Dana's own sheet, PCC 89 vol. II p. 656 (naId 502963402, object 262, file 407345), one AI reading at reduced size: alphabets a = 15, 6, 20 and n = 1, 19, 6; Adams 30 61 92, Administration 1 2 3; Franklin 123 154 185, Minister 7 8 9; the example and its numbers; 'This goes by a private & safe hand' (the bearer J. Q. Adams is from Dana's letter at p. 648, not from the sheet). The numbers follow their word (Army 35, America 33; 'America. 33. 64. 95'), so 137 and 168 are Minister. 216-263 are sixteen words, Spanish to Warontzow; 264-305 are blank. Object 207 of item 109 laid beside transcription.txt line by line: 215 numbers, all 208 agree, the seven completed numbers are there. So 31, 137 and 168 are read with the writer's own table and the seven numbers are confirmed from a clerk's copy of the despatch (not the triplicate's own sheet). 29 stays open. reading.md recounted: 52 words, 5 holes (In; is, any, irresistable, influence with a slip or the skipped key position), 0.904: read in part. Not checked: the whole sheet number by number; the other words; which copy the clerk had; the original and duplicate of No. 23. No person has checked an image.

outcome.method_basis: The WIN table was recovered from the eight cipher lines alone (period and alphabet size by index of coincidence, shifts by scoring). The three word codes 31, 137 and 168 are not from the ciphertext: they are read with the writer's own key, Dana's table of October 1782 found in the same volume (PCC 89 vol. II p. 656, Brice Dudout; viewed 24 Nov 2026; clerk's copy in PCC item 109, Andrew Beling). 29 stays without value.
outcome.fraction_read_source: Tokens: 214 of 215 given a value (211 letter positions, of which 7 cut or missing on the triplicate are taken from the clerk's transcript in PCC item 109; 31, 137, 168 from Dana's table; 29 open). Words (README rule, recounted 24 Nov 2026 with research/reading_audit/v2_score.holes on reading.md): 52 words, 5 holes (In; is, any, irresistable, influence), read_share 0.904. If the seven numbers from the clerk's copy were counted as supplied, 42 of 52 = 0.808. docs/_check_reading.py on reading.md: readable, clean share 0.8, hole rate 0.07.

texts.label: No. 23, St Petersburg, 6 Apr 1783 (O.S.), PCC 89 vol. 2 p. 730
texts.summary: Dana, waiting in vain for the Russian court to receive him, explains why he cannot predict the outcome: in an Administration not guided by settled principles or system nothing can be counted on, what the Minister adopt in this hour may be opposed by another influence in the next, and properly speaking there is no Minister here. One group (29) is open.
texts.note: Recounted 24 Nov 2026: 52 words, 5 holes (In, from the open group 29; is, any, irresistable, influence, each with a letter Dana enciphered wrongly or after a skipped key position, bracketed in reading.md). Administration and Minister are read from Dana's own table (key.txt). The seven numbers cut or missing on the triplicate are taken from the clerk's transcript in PCC item 109 and are not marked. Dana's spelling kept. The reading_review below is of 14 Nov 2026 and describes the file before this change (0.855, four groups open); the sentences are the same.

reading_review.note: Read reading.md against decryption.txt line by line. Four coherent English sentences; the letter stream divides into words without remainder; seven letters completed at a cut number or supplied at a line end are bracketed, four code groups are left as [29], [31], [137], [168]. The reading normalises one spelling (decode irresistable, reading irresistible), as its header says. read_share 0.855, so read in part. Image not re-opened in this pass.

texts.label: Dana to Livingston, St Petersburg, 6/17 Apr 1783: independent reading by Brice Dudout with Dana's table of Oct 1782
texts.summary: Brice Dudout's reading of the same eight lines with Dana's own table (PCC 89 vol. II p. 656): the three word codes read as Administration and Minister.

reading_review.note: Read dudout/reading.md against dudout/decryption.txt. The same four sentences, coherent, with the word codes filled from Dana's table of October 1782 as his README reports (31 Administration, 137 and 168 Minister); deduced letters in braces, corrected slips in ‹›, Dana's spelling kept. The table sheet (PCC 89 vol. II p. 656) was not viewed in this pass, so the three code values rest on the contributor's report.

outcome.notes: Contributed by WAINUT (catalogue 485). The decryption needs ten interventions out of 211 letter positions (three slips, four completed cut numbers, three supplied line-end letters) plus one skipped key position; all are explicit in decrypt.py. No earlier decipherment found; the search was not exhaustive, so first_break = true stands until the MHS Dana Papers and the original and duplicate of No. 23 are checked. The PCC 59 key sheet 'No. 1' was found and checked after the break and is a different scheme, so the method stays ciphertext-only. 24 Nov 2026: Dana's own table (PCC 89 vol. II p. 656) viewed and its copy in PCC item 109 found by Andrew Beling (issue #898): 31, 137, 168 read with it; the seven completed numbers confirmed by the item 109 transcript of No. 23 (a clerk's copy), so that gap is closed; 29 is the one open group. The table reading is Brice Dudout's, the break WAINUT's. All image readings are AI readings. No site page exists yet.
